sermon:
## Tested, and Not Left Alone
*Why the fire is the favor, not its absence*

**Text:** James 1 · **Supporting:** Job 23:10 · 1 Peter 1:6-7 · Romans 5:3-5 · Matthew 7:24-27

The letter opens to people who have lost their homes. "To the twelve tribes in the Dispersion", scattered, displaced, the kind of believers whose lives have come apart at the seams. And the first word James gives them is not comfort. It is a command to count.

**The trial is not the verdict.**
James writes, "Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness" (James 1:2-3). Read it slowly. He does not say *if* you meet trials. He says *when*. The trial is assumed. What is not assumed is the response, and the response he asks for is the hardest thing imaginable to a scattered, frightened church, joy. Not because the pain is good. Because the pain is doing something. The word he uses for testing is the word for what fire does to metal, it does not destroy the gold, it proves it. Job knew this before James wrote it down. "When he has tried me, I shall come out as gold" (Job 23:10). Peter says the same, that the tested genuineness of your faith is "more precious than gold that perishes" (1 Peter 1:7). Three witnesses, one verdict. The fire is not the sign that God has left. The fire is the sign that God is at work on something He intends to keep. We read suffering as abandonment. James reads it as attention.

And then he says the thing that turns the whole logic of the trial inside out. "Let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing" (James 1:4). Lacking in nothing. The thing you are sure the trial is taking from you is the very thing James says it is producing in you. We come to suffering certain it is subtraction. James calls it the only road to completion there is. There is a kind of maturity God grows in no greenhouse, it grows only in weather. The man who has never been tested has never been proven, and the church that has never bled has nothing to say to a bleeding world. The fire is not the interruption of the work. The fire is the work.

**Ask, and do not stagger.**
But the scattered believer does not feel like gold being refined. He feels like a man who has run out of answers. So James turns immediately to wisdom: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him" (James 1:5). Notice what God does not do. He does not lecture. He does not make you earn it. He does not bring up the last time you asked and then ignored what He said. He gives, *without reproach*. There is no other giver in your life like this. Every other source of help keeps a ledger. God keeps a door open. Paul traces the same chain James does: "suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope" (Romans 5:3-4). The wisdom is not a way around the trial. It is the thing the trial is for. And here is the one condition, "let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind" (James 1:6). Not a perfect faith. A faith that does not keep one foot in the world's door while knocking on God's. The double-minded man, James says, is "unstable in all his ways" (James 1:8), and the instability is not in the storm around him but in the divided wanting inside him. He prays to God and hedges with the world, and then he wonders why he feels tossed. He is tossed because he is two men asking for one thing.

And lest the trial harden into bitterness, lest the tested believer begin to suspect the testing God of cruelty, James cuts that lie off at the root. "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God,' for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one" (James 1:13). The God who tests your faith to prove it is never the author of the evil that would destroy it. "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change" (James 1:17). The Father does not flicker. The same God stands behind the gift and the trial, and not once behind the temptation. Hold both, or you will either resent Him for the fire or excuse yourself for the fall.

**Hearing is not having.**
Then comes the turn that indicts every one of us who has ever sat in a pew and felt informed. "Be doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves" (James 1:22). Deceiving yourselves. The self-deception of the religious man is the most respectable sin in the church, because it looks exactly like devotion. I have preached sermons I did not obey. I have studied a text on Saturday and walked past the very thing it commanded on Monday, and called the studying obedience. That is the mirror James holds up: "For if anyone is a hearer of the word and not a doer, he is like a man who looks intently at his natural face in a mirror. For he looks at himself and goes away and at once forgets what he was like" (James 1:23-24). The word showed him who he was. He liked the information and left the man unchanged. Jesus drew the line in the same place, two builders, one storm, the difference not in what they heard but in what they did with it (Matthew 7:24-27). The house that stood and the house that fell heard the identical words. One built on them. One admired them.

And James will not leave the doing vague, where we prefer it, because vague obedience is the kind that costs nothing. He names it: "Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world" (James 1:27). The orphan and the widow, the two people in the ancient world with no one to protect them, no standing, nothing to give back. That is where James says the word you heard becomes the life you live, or proves it never landed at all. A man raised without a father hears that verse in a particular register. The God who tests faith in the fire defines pure religion as going to the very ones the fire left alone.

So here is the weight the scattered church was meant to carry out of chapter one, and the weight we carry still. The trial that found you is not proof that God turned away, it is the furnace where He proves what He will not abandon. The wisdom you lack is one honest, undivided prayer away from a Father who will not shame you for asking. And the word you heard this morning will save no one who only hears it. The deceived man is not the one who rejected the truth. He is the one who agreed with it and went home unchanged, certain he had received something, holding nothing.

Hearing is not having.

## The Sin of the Welcome Mat
*How the church learned to seat the cross by the wealth of the room*

**Text:** James 2:1-13 · **Supporting:** Leviticus 19:18 · 1 Corinthians 1:26-29 · Proverbs 14:31 · Matthew 25:40

James sets the scene in a single sentence, and it is a scene we recognize because we have staged it. A rich man walks into the assembly with a gold ring and fine clothing, and a poor man walks in behind him in filthy rags, and the church, the gathered people of the Lord of glory, decides where each of them sits.

**Partiality is theology, badly done.**
"My brothers, show no partiality as you hold the faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory" (James 2:1). He binds the two together on purpose. You cannot hold faith in a crucified Lord and a velvet rope at the same time. The Lord of glory had no place to lay His head. He was born in a borrowed stall and buried in a borrowed tomb, and the church that worships Him cannot turn around and rank the room by its tailoring. And yet, James says, you say to the rich man, "You sit here in a good place," while you say to the poor man, "You stand over there" (James 2:3). Then comes the verdict, and it is sharper than a complaint about manners: "have you not then made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?" (James 2:4). Judges. With evil thoughts. The man sorting the room by its clothing thinks he is being prudent. He is being a judge, and he has seated himself on a bench God never gave him, ruling by a standard God never used. Worse, the standard he is using is precisely backward. James points it out with a bluntness that should sting any congregation chasing the wealthy donor: "Are not the rich the ones who oppress you, and the ones who drag you into court? Are they not the ones who blaspheme the honorable name by which you were called?" (James 2:6-7). The very people you are bending over to honor are often the ones whose power is built on grinding down the very people you are shaming. You are flattering the wolf and shooing the lamb, and calling it good order.

**God has already chosen, and not as you would have.**
"Listen, my beloved brothers, has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom?" (James 2:5). The room you are sorting, God has already walked through, and He did not seat people the way you do. Paul saw the same divine pattern and named it without flinching: "Not many of you were wise according to worldly standards, not many were powerful, not many were of noble birth. But God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise" (1 Corinthians 1:26-27). The church that honors the wealthy and shames the poor is not merely rude. It is contradicting the God whose kingdom is built out of exactly the people it is embarrassed to seat. "Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the Lord," Proverbs says (Proverbs 14:31, paraphrasing 19:17), and "whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker." You are not just slighting the man in the rags. You are insulting the One who made him and chose him.

**Mercy triumphs over judgment.**
Then James names the law that governs all of it: "If you really fulfill the royal law according to the Scripture, You shall love your neighbor as yourself, you are doing well" (James 2:8, quoting Leviticus 19:18). The royal law. Not a suggestion for the well-meaning, the law of the King. And to break it at one point, James says, is to become accountable for all of it: "For whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become accountable for all of it" (James 2:10). We treat sin like a checklist, where partiality is a minor box left unchecked against a long column of boxes filled. James treats the law as a single garment, pull one thread and the whole thing is torn, because the law is not a list of disconnected rules but the single will of one God. The God who said do not murder is the God who said do not show partiality, and to despise the poor man is to despise the Lawgiver, not just the law.

I have done this. I have warmed to the visitor whose presence flattered the church and given the harder, poorer, more demanding person the thin smile and the back row. I have noticed which guest could fund the building and which guest would only ever need from us, and I have felt my welcome adjust before I could stop it. I have called it discernment. It was partiality wearing discernment's coat. And the Lord I claim to serve said the test of the last day would turn on exactly this, "as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me" (Matthew 25:40). The man in the rags was Christ in the room, and the church did not see Him. We were so busy reading the clothing that we missed the King who told us He would be wearing exactly those rags.

So James closes the section where every honest reckoning with our own judgment must close: "So speak and so act as those who are to be judged under the law of liberty. For judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy" (James 2:12-13). The measure you used on the poor man at the door is the measure waiting for you. The bench you climbed onto to sort the room has a higher bench above it, and on that one you are the defendant. There is only one thing that overrules a verdict like that, and it is not your good manners or your church growth or the comfort of the people who could afford the good seats.

Mercy triumphs over judgment.

## The Faith That Does Nothing
*On the belief that says all the right words and moves nothing*

**Text:** James 2:14-26 · **Supporting:** Genesis 15:6 · Joshua 2:11 · Matthew 7:21 · Ephesians 2:8-10

James asks a question that has frightened the church for two thousand years, and it deserves to. "What good is it, my brothers, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can that faith save him?" (James 2:14). Notice the precision. He does not ask whether faith saves. He asks whether *that* faith, the kind that says and does not do, can save anyone at all.

**A faith you can only hear is not a faith you can trust.**
He gives the case so plainly no one can hide from it. "If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacking in daily food, and one of you says to them, 'Go in peace, be warmed and filled,' without giving them the things needed for the body, what good is that?" (James 2:15-16). The man said all the right things. He blessed the cold and fed the hungry with sentences. He prayed a warm prayer over an empty stomach and walked away feeling generous. And the verdict lands: "So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead" (James 2:17). Dead. Not weak. Not immature. Dead, the way a body is dead.

Then James voices the objection before we can, because he knows the reply forming in the back of the room. "But someone will say, 'You have faith and I have works.' Show me your faith apart from your works, and I will show you my faith by my works" (James 2:18). It is a dare, and it cannot be met. You cannot show faith with no works. There is nothing to point at. Faith with no works is a claim about an invisible thing with no visible evidence, and James says that is not a quiet faith, it is a dead one. Then he presses harder, against the man who is proud of his orthodoxy: "You believe that God is one; you do well. Even the demons believe, and shudder" (James 2:19). There is a faith that gets the doctrine exactly right and changes nothing, and James says the demons have it. They are not atheists. They confess perfect monotheism. They are theologically precise and eternally lost, and at least they have the honesty to shudder, which is more than the comfortable orthodox man in the pew can say. Right belief that produces no obedience is not the beginning of salvation. It is the religion of hell.

**The two witnesses: a patriarch and a prostitute.**
Then James calls two witnesses to the stand, and the pairing is deliberate and scandalous. First, Abraham, the father of the faithful. "Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered up his son Isaac on the altar?" (James 2:21). This is the same Abraham of whom Genesis says, "he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). James is not contradicting Genesis; he is completing it. The faith Genesis recorded was real, and the altar on Moriah is where that faith showed its face. "Faith was active along with his works, and faith was completed by his works" (James 2:22). Then, in the same breath, a woman the synagogue would never have seated near Abraham, Rahab, a Canaanite prostitute. "Was not also Rahab the prostitute justified by works when she received the messengers and sent them out by another way?" (James 2:25). She had said it herself, hadn't she, "the Lord your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath" (Joshua 2:11). But the words alone would have left the spies on her doorstep to die. The faith was proven when she hid them and risked her life. A patriarch and a prostitute, and the same verdict over both: the faith that saved them was the faith that did something.

**Dead faith saves no one.**
Now turn the mirror, because James means it for the man in the pew, not the man in the Bible. I have met the dead faith, and I have preached to it, and some Sundays I have carried it. It is the faith that knows the catechism and skips the neighbor. It signs the doctrinal statement and never opens the wallet. It can defend penal substitution and will not forgive a brother. Jesus warned of this faith in the plainest words He ever spoke: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father" (Matthew 7:21). Saying *Lord, Lord* is the faith that does nothing. And lest anyone hear James and conclude we are saved by our works, hear Paul standing beside him, not against him: "by grace you have been saved through faith... not a result of works." And then the very next breath, "created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them" (Ephesians 2:8-10). The works do not earn the grace. The works are the proof the grace arrived.

And here is where Abraham and Rahab point past themselves to the only One whose faith and works were ever perfectly one. The patriarch raised the knife and the son was spared; on a darker hill the Father did not spare His own Son, and the faith of Jesus was completed not in a willingness to slay but in a willingness to be slain. "He humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:8). That is faith made perfect in works, the only living faith the world has ever fully seen. The faith that saves you is not your achievement; it is your grip on His. But a real grip on a living Christ has hands, and those hands feed the hungry brother they used to bless with sentences. A faith joined to the obedient Christ cannot stay a corpse.

So James leaves us with a body on the floor and a question we would rather not answer. "For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead" (James 2:26). The faith you are counting on, has it moved anything? Has it fed anyone, forgiven anyone, cost you anything? Or does it only speak, bless the hungry with sentences, recite the creed, and go home unchanged? Examine it honestly, because there is a faith that says all the right words over a corpse.

Dead faith saves no one.

## The Small Fire
*The smallest member of the body, and the whole life it burns down*

**Text:** James 3:1-12 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 18:21 · Matthew 12:34 · Psalm 39:1 · Genesis 1:27

James takes the smallest thing in the human body and shows you it is steering your entire life. "How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire. And the tongue is a fire" (James 3:5-6). We treat words as the light currency of life, cheap, recoverable, forgotten by morning. James treats them as arson.

**The small thing that steers the large.**
But James does not begin with the fire. He begins with a warning to the men most certain they have their words under control, the teachers. "Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness" (James 3:1). We. He includes himself. The man writing the sermon on the tongue puts his own mouth first under the judgment. Then he stacks the images so you cannot miss the scale. "If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs" (James 3:3-4). A bit. A rudder. A tongue. The smallest part, and it sets the course of the whole. We measure a life by its large moments, the career, the marriage, the public decisions. James says the life was steered all along by the thing you said in the kitchen, the thing you posted at midnight, the thing you let slip about a brother and never took back. Solomon said it first: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (Proverbs 18:21). Not influence. Not impact. Death and life. The rudder is small enough to ignore and strong enough to run the ship onto the rocks, and most lives wreck not on one great sin but on a thousand small sentences that pointed the whole vessel at the reef.

**No man tames it, and the spring tells the truth.**
Then James says the thing that should empty out every self-improvement scheme we have ever brought to our own mouths. "Every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison" (James 3:7-8). Restless, it never sleeps, never finally submits, waits for the moment of fatigue or anger and then it is loose again. Man has broken the horse and the lion and the serpent. He has put the elephant in a circus ring and the orca in a tank. Man cannot break his own mouth. The strongest evidence in Scripture that we are not the masters of ourselves we imagine ourselves to be is this single member we cannot govern. And the reason James gives is not a reason about the tongue at all, it is a reason about the heart behind it. "With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God" (James 3:9). There it is. We praise God in the same hour we tear down the man God made in His own image (Genesis 1:27). "From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so" (James 3:10). Jesus located the leak exactly where James does: "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks" (Matthew 12:34). The tongue is not the problem. The tongue is the witness. It testifies, every day, against the heart that thought it was hidden.

**Your mouth tells the truth.**
Then the verdict, in the form of a question no honest man can dodge: "Can a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water?" (James 3:11). No. The spring tells the truth about its source. And I will tell you where this finds me, because the kill switch James is describing is one I cannot reach. I have stood in the pulpit and blessed the God who made men, and sat in the car afterward and cursed one of them. I have prayed for a person Sunday morning and dismantled him Sunday night, and felt no contradiction at all, because the heart is that divided and the mouth is that honest about it. David knew the trap and could only beg his way out of it: "I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I will guard my mouth with a muzzle" (Psalm 39:1). A muzzle. He did not trust himself with an open mouth, and he was a man after God's own heart. If David needed a muzzle, the man who thinks he has his tongue under control has simply not been listening to himself.

There is one mouth in all of history out of which only fresh water ever ran. "No deceit was found in his mouth" (1 Peter 2:22). When He was reviled, He did not revile in return. The crowd cursed Him from the same human nature that curses one another, and from the cross the only words He had for them were words that blessed, "Father, forgive them" (Luke 23:34). That is the spring James says the rest of us cannot be. And the gospel is not that you will finally tame your tongue by trying harder; it is that the Word who tamed His own took the curse your mouth deserved and offers you, in exchange, a new heart from which a new spring can run. The blessing you fake on Sunday, He can make true on Tuesday, but only by changing the source, never by guarding the mouth.

So do not leave this text resolving to talk better. That is the horse-and-lion strategy, and James already told you it fails. The mouth cannot be reformed from the mouth. The spring runs salt because the source is salt, and only the One who can make a new heart can make a new spring. Until then, your words are not the small, forgettable thing you have been treating them as. They are the steady, daily, unwelcome witness to what you actually are underneath the blessing you offer on Sunday.

Your mouth tells the truth.

## Two Wisdoms
*One looks like cleverness and breeds chaos. One looks like weakness and grows peace.*

**Text:** James 3:13-18 · **Supporting:** Proverbs 3:7 · 1 Corinthians 1:25 · Galatians 5:22-23 · Matthew 11:29

James asks a question and then refuses to let you answer it the way you want to. "Who is wise and understanding among you?" (James 3:13). Every hand goes up in the heart, even when it stays down at the side. We all believe we are the wise one in the room. James says: prove it, and prove it not with your argument but with your life.

**Wisdom is shown, not claimed.**
"By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom" (James 3:13). Show. Not state. This is the same logic James has run through the whole letter, faith shown by works, religion shown in care for the orphan, the mouth showing the heart. Now wisdom, shown by conduct. The first mark of the false wisdom is that it talks about how wise it is. The true wisdom is quiet enough to be missed, it has *meekness* in it, the same meekness Jesus claimed for Himself: "learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart" (Matthew 11:29). The wisest man who ever lived described Himself as gentle and lowly, which ought to end forever our confusion of wisdom with cleverness. Then James names the counterfeit without mercy: "But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth" (James 3:14). The two words are the tell, jealousy and selfish ambition. The man who is always comparing and always climbing thinks he is shrewd. He is not. He is bitter and ambitious, and he has dressed it up as discernment. And when his strategies blow up the people around him, he calls the wreckage the cost of leadership. James calls it something else.

**The wisdom from below, and where it leads.**
Then James does something startling. He gives the false wisdom a pedigree, and traces it down through three descending floors. "This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic" (James 3:15). Earthly, it belongs to the dirt, it reaches no higher than the world's own logic. Unspiritual, it has no part in the Spirit who searches the deep things of God. Demonic, and there James stops the descent, at the bottom, naming the true author of a cleverness that exists to win and to climb. And he names its fruit before you can argue: "For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice" (James 3:16). Disorder. The marriage that is always negotiating who is right. The church that is always managing factions. The workplace that runs on rivalry. We call it ambition and admire it. James calls it the visible evidence that a demonic wisdom is doing exactly what it does, breaking things apart. The world is certain this kind of shrewdness is strength. Paul met that certainty head-on: "the foolishness of God is wiser than men, and the weakness of God is stronger than men" (1 Corinthians 1:25). The cleverness the world crowns, heaven calls foolishness.

**Wisdom is known by fruit.**
Then the wisdom from above, and notice James does not define it, he describes its harvest, because that is the only way you can ever recognize it. "The wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere" (James 3:17). Read that list against your own week. Pure, single-hearted, not running an angle. Peaceable, not needing to win. Open to reason, able to be wrong without dying. Full of mercy, bent toward the failing, not the impressive. This is the same harvest Paul names from the Spirit: "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). Two apostles, one orchard. And here is where it implicates me, and the men I train, and every leader who has confused being shrewd with being wise. I have made decisions that produced disorder and called the disorder a sign of how hard the truth is. I have nursed a comparison in my chest and named it standards. Proverbs warned me before I started: "Be not wise in your own eyes; fear the Lord, and turn away from evil" (Proverbs 3:7). The wise-in-his-own-eyes man is the demonic wisdom's favorite disguise, and it fits a pastor as well as anyone.

And here the two wisdoms finally stand before a cross, where the world's shrewdness met the wisdom of God and called it foolishness. The clever men of that day, the ones with bitter jealousy and selfish ambition, the ones managing the room and protecting their position, looked at a crucified Galilean and saw a fool destroyed by his own weakness. Paul names exactly what they missed: "Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God" (1 Corinthians 1:24). The wisdom from above is not an idea James is describing; it is a Person who was pure and peaceable and full of mercy all the way to a Roman cross, who would rather be slain than be proven right, who sowed in peace the only harvest of righteousness the world will ever see. The harvest of His life was a saved people. Measure your wisdom against His, and the cleverness you were proud of looks like the very thing that nailed Him there.

So James will not let you settle the question by feeling clever. "A harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace" (James 3:18). Look at the field your life is growing. If it is full of rivalry and division and the wreckage of relationships you outmaneuvered, you may be very shrewd, and you are not wise, not by the only measure heaven uses. The wisdom from above does not announce itself. It shows up as a man who is hard to provoke and quick to forgive, who would rather be at peace than be proven right, and who, when you look at the harvest of his life, has left things more whole than he found them.

Wisdom is known by fruit.

## Friendship With the World
*The war you keep losing is the one inside your own desires*

**Text:** James 4 · **Supporting:** 1 John 2:15-16 · Proverbs 3:34 · Exodus 20:5 · Matthew 6:24

James asks where the fighting comes from, and his answer does not point out the window at the people you are fighting. It points back into your own chest. "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1). The conflict in the church, in the marriage, in the home, James traces it to a battlefield you have been mistaking for a neighbor.

**The war is inside, and so is the silence over your prayers.**
"You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel" (James 4:2). The desire that cannot get what it wants becomes the rage that destroys what it can reach. We always think the conflict is about the other person, his stubbornness, her selfishness, their refusal to see it our way. James drags the cause back inside the house and sets it down in our own chest. The fight in the marriage is a war between two sets of cravings that each insist on being satisfied. The split in the church is a hundred private appetites colliding in a public room. You did not start fighting because someone wronged you. You started fighting because you wanted something you could not have, and the person in front of you was in the way. And then James says something about prayer that should stop every disappointed petitioner cold. "You do not have, because you do not ask. You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions" (James 4:2-3). There are two reasons your prayers go unanswered, and James names both. You did not ask. Or you asked, but the prayer was just your appetite wearing reverent language, a request for God to fund the very passions at war inside you. We blame the silence of heaven. James says examine the motive of the asking. Often the prayer was never aimed at God at all. It was aimed at the self, addressed to God.

**Friendship with the world is enmity with God.**
Then the verse that names the whole disease, and James uses the word the prophets used for covenant betrayal, adultery. "You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God" (James 4:4). This is not a warning against the world's pleasures in some narrow sense. It is the charge of spiritual unfaithfulness against people who thought they could keep God and the world both. John named the same triangle: "the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life" (1 John 2:16), and said plainly, "If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him" (1 John 2:15). Jesus had already closed the door on the both-and: "No one can serve two masters... You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24). And James reaches back into the law itself, to the jealousy of God at Sinai, "I the Lord your God am a jealous God" (Exodus 20:5), when he writes that the Spirit God made to dwell in us "yearns jealously" (James 4:5). The God who saved you will not share you. He is not insecure. He is faithful, and He will not call your divided heart anything other than what it is.

**Humble yourself. He lifts.**
And then, in the middle of the most severe paragraph in the letter, the door opens. "But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble'" (James 4:6, quoting Proverbs 3:34). He gives *more* grace, more than the adultery, more than the wasted prayers, more than the years of friendship with the world. There is more grace in God than there is unfaithfulness in you. But it runs in only one direction. It flows down, to the low place, to the humble, and it runs away from the proud the way water runs off a peak. So James commands the descent: "Submit yourselves therefore to God... Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded" (James 4:7-8). I know this double-mindedness from the inside. I have prayed for the growth of a work and wanted the glory of it. I have asked God to bless what I had already decided to do for myself. I have wished to be a friend of God on Sunday and a friend of the world's approval every other day, and called the arrangement balance. It is not balance. James calls it adultery, and the only cure he offers is not a better strategy. It is a man on his face.

And the One who calls us down to that low place went lower first. The grace that flows only to the humble flows from a Lord who "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Philippians 2:7), who came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom (Mark 10:45). The descent James commands, submit, draw near, humble yourself, is not a technique we perform to climb; it is the shape of the Christ we are joined to. He went down to the cross, and God exalted Him to the highest place. That is the pattern, and there is no other way up. The friendship with the world that ruins your prayers and your marriage and your church will not be defeated by winning. It is defeated the way He defeated it, by going low, by losing, by trusting the Father who lifts the humbled. Faith in this Lord is shown in the bent knee, not the raised fist.

So the chapter that began with quarrels ends with the only posture that ends them: "Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you" (James 4:10). You have been trying to win the war by winning the fights, outmaneuvering the people, getting the desire met, making the prayer work harder. James says the war is inside you, the desire is the enemy, and the only way up is down. Stop climbing. Get low. The hand you have been fighting to lift yourself is not the hand that lifts.

Humble yourself. He lifts.

## Until the Lord Comes
*Patience for the wronged, judgment for the hoarder, and a church that prays*

**Text:** James 5 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 24:14-15 · Job 1:21 · Matthew 24:42 · 1 Kings 17-18

James ends his letter the way the prophets ended their oracles, with the rich man's gold rusting in his hand and the poor man told to wait a little longer for God. "Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you" (James 5:1). The last chapter is about the long stretch between the wrong done and the Lord who will right it.

**The wages that cry out.**
James does not condemn wealth in the abstract. He condemns what the hoarder did with it and to whom. "Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts" (James 5:4). The withheld wage has a voice, and it has reached the ears of God. This is not new law, it is Moses, who commanded, "You shall give him his wages on the same day... lest he cry against you to the Lord, and you be guilty of sin" (Deuteronomy 24:15). The defrauded worker cannot reach the rich man's lawyer or his gate. He can reach God's ear, and God hears the cry the powerful never have to answer for in this life. "You have laid up treasure in the last days," James says (James 5:3), the cruelest irony, a man storing up money in the very season the world is ending. He thought he was getting ahead. He was filling a barn the night before the harvest of judgment.

**Be patient, like the farmer.**
Then James turns from the oppressor to the oppressed, from the howling rich to the waiting church, and his word to the wronged is the hardest word of all: wait. "Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains" (James 5:7). The farmer is the picture, because the farmer cannot make it rain and cannot make it grow. He puts the seed in the ground and he waits on a God who controls the weather. That is the believer who has been defrauded and cannot get justice, he commits the harvest to the One who sends the rain and he waits. James calls up the prophets as his witnesses to suffering, and then Job: "You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful" (James 5:11). The Job who, stripped of everything, said, "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord" (Job 1:21). The patience James asks for is not passive. It is the active trust that the Judge is at the door, "the Judge is standing at the door" (James 5:9), exactly as Jesus warned: "Stay awake, for you do not know on what day your Lord is coming" (Matthew 24:42).

**The church that prays until then.**
And what does the waiting church do in the meantime? It does not grit its teeth in isolation. It prays, over everything, for everyone. "Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise. Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him" (James 5:13-14). The whole life of the community runs through prayer, the sick, the sinning, the suffering, the glad. "Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working" (James 5:16). Then James, who has spent five chapters demanding a faith that does something, ends with the most ordinary doer in the Bible, a praying man. "Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain" (James 5:17). A man with a nature like ours. Not a superhuman. A frightened, discouraged prophet who once asked God to let him die, and when he prayed, the heavens closed and opened (1 Kings 17-18). I have been a man who preached patience to others while privately demanding that God hurry. I have told suffering people to wait on the Lord and then refused to wait myself, treating prayer as the thing I do when the strategies fail. James ends his letter taking that back from me. Prayer is not the last resort of the church. It is the work of the waiting church, and it is powerful in the hands of ordinary, weak, righteous men.

And the patience James asks for is not a stoic's clenched jaw; it is staked on a Person who is coming. "The coming of the Lord is at hand" (James 5:8). The farmer waits because he trusts the One who sends the rain. The defrauded believer waits because he trusts the One who was Himself defrauded, sold for thirty pieces of silver, denied his wages of justice, condemned by the rich and powerful of his day, and who "continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Peter 2:23). Jesus did not avenge Himself. He waited on the Father, and the Father vindicated Him at an empty tomb. That resurrection is why the patience holds, the Judge at the door is the risen Christ, and the wrongs stored up against the oppressor and the wages crying out from the field will all be settled by the One who already absorbed the worst injustice the world could do and walked out the other side. Patience like that is not passivity. It is faith in a coming Lord, shown in a praying, waiting, hoping church.

So the letter closes with a church told to hold on. The wrong you suffered is heard. The wage withheld is crying out to a God who has not gone deaf. The Judge is at the door, and the rain is coming for the patient farmer, and in the long meantime you are not to grit your teeth alone, you are to pray, confess, sing, and call the elders, because the prayer of an ordinary man still moves the hand of God. The coming of the Lord is at hand. Live like it is.

Be patient. He is near.
